specStatements.text: Scalar quantities have magnitude only.
Vector quantities have magnitude and an associated direction.
A vector quantity may be represented by an arrow. The length of the arrow represents the magnitude, and the direction of the arrow the direction of the vector quantity.
A force is a push or pull that acts on an object due to the interaction with another object. All forces between objects are either:
• contact forces – the objects are physically touching
• non-contact forces – the objects are physically separated.
Examples of contact forces include friction, air resistance, tension and normal contact force.
Examples of non-contact forces are gravitational force, electrostatic force and magnetic force.
Force is a vector quantity.
Students should be able to describe the interaction between pairs of objects which produce a force on each object. The forces to be represented as vectors.
Weight is the force acting on an object due to gravity. The force of gravity close to the Earth is due to the gravitational field around the Earth.
The weight of an object depends on the gravitational field strength at the point where the object is.
The weight of an object can be calculated using the equation:
weight = mass × gravitational field strength
[W = m g]
weight, W, in newtons, N
mass, m, in kilograms, kg
gravitational field strength, g, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg (In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength (g) will be given.)
The weight of an object may be considered to act at a single point referred to as the object’s ‘centre of mass’.
The weight of an object and the mass of an object are directly proportional.
Weight is measured using a calibrated spring-balance (a newtonmeter).
A number of forces acting on an object may be replaced by a single force that has the same effect as all the original forces acting together. This single force is called the resultant force.
Students should be able to calculate the resultant of two forces that act in a straight line.
(HT only) Students should be able to:
• describe examples of the forces acting on an isolated object or system
• use free body diagrams to describe qualitatively examples where several forces lead to a resultant force on an object, including balanced forces when the resultant force is zero.
(HT only) A single force can be resolved into two components acting at right angles to each other. The two component forces together have the same effect as the single force.

(HT only) Students should be able to use vector diagrams to illustrate resolution of forces, equilibrium situations and determine the resultant of two forces, to include both magnitude and direction (scale drawings only).

scopeNotes.statement: (In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength (g) will be given.)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item asks a student to recall a value of g, and no item assumes one. Every calculation in this material states the gravitational field strength inside the question stem (9.8 N/kg for the Earth-based examples, and an unstated value on an unnamed planet for the proportionality item, which is solved by ratio rather than by a remembered number). Where a comparison between the Earth and the Moon is made, it is made qualitatively — the Moon's field strength is described as smaller, and no numerical value is supplied or expected. Students are taught what g means and its unit, N/kg, because the specification states that; they are never taught that g has a number they must memorise.

The Higher Tier vector-diagram content is taught and assessed as scale drawing only. The item on the resultant of two perpendicular forces states explicitly that a scale drawing has been used, and the answer is the value read from that drawing; no trigonometry, no Pythagoras' theorem and no algebraic resolution formula (F cos θ, F sin θ) appears anywhere in this material. Resolution of a force into two components at right angles is treated qualitatively — what the components are and what they do together — and equilibrium is treated as the geometric property of a closed vector diagram, not as a set of simultaneous equations. Angles are never asked for as calculated values.

concepts.definition: A quantity that has magnitude only. A scalar is fully described by a number and a unit, with no direction attached to it.
A quantity that has magnitude and an associated direction. Two vectors of the same magnitude are different quantities if their directions differ.

concepts.term: Representing a vector by an arrow
concepts.definition: A vector quantity may be represented by an arrow. The length of the arrow represents the magnitude, and the direction of the arrow the direction of the vector quantity. A longer arrow therefore means a larger quantity, and two arrows drawn to the same scale can be compared directly.

A force is a push or pull that acts on an object due to the interaction with another object. A force never belongs to a single object on its own — it always arises from an interaction between two objects.
A force in which the objects are physically touching.
A force in which the objects are physically separated.

Examples of contact forces include friction, air resistance, tension and normal contact force. In each case the two interacting objects are physically touching — including air resistance, where the object is touching the air it moves through.
Examples of non-contact forces are gravitational force, electrostatic force and magnetic force. These act between objects that are physically separated.
Force is a vector quantity. A force is only fully described when both its magnitude in newtons and its direction are given, and it may be represented by an arrow drawn in that direction.

concepts.term: Interaction between a pair of objects
concepts.definition: When two objects interact, a force is produced on each of the two objects. Describing an interaction means naming both objects and stating the force each one experiences, with both forces represented as vectors.

Weight is the force acting on an object due to gravity. The force of gravity close to the Earth is due to the gravitational field around the Earth. Weight is a force, so it is a vector measured in newtons.

The weight of an object depends on the gravitational field strength at the point where the object is. The same object has a different weight at a place where the gravitational field strength is different, even though its mass is unchanged.

weight = mass × gravitational field strength, written W = m g. This equation must be recalled and applied. weight, W, in newtons, N; mass, m, in kilograms, kg; gravitational field strength, g, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg.
The unit of weight: weight, W, in newtons, N. Because weight is a force, every weight is quoted in newtons.
The unit of mass: mass, m, in kilograms, kg. Mass must be in kilograms before it is substituted into W = m g.

The unit of gravitational field strength: gravitational field strength, g, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg. It states how many newtons of weight each kilogram of mass has at that point. In any calculation the value of g will be given.
The weight of an object may be considered to act at a single point referred to as the object's 'centre of mass'. On a diagram, the weight is therefore drawn as one arrow starting at that point.

concepts.term: Weight is directly proportional to mass
concepts.definition: The weight of an object and the mass of an object are directly proportional. At a fixed gravitational field strength, doubling the mass doubles the weight, and a graph of weight against mass is a straight line passing through the origin.
Weight is measured using a calibrated spring-balance (a newtonmeter). The scale is calibrated in newtons, because weight is a force.
A number of forces acting on an object may be replaced by a single force that has the same effect as all the original forces acting together. This single force is called the resultant force.

concepts.term: Resultant of two forces in a straight line
concepts.definition: For two forces acting along the same straight line, forces acting in the same direction are added and forces acting in opposite directions are subtracted. The resultant must be given with its direction as well as its magnitude, because force is a vector.

A diagram showing only the forces that act on one chosen object, each drawn as an arrow whose length represents the magnitude and whose direction represents the direction of the force. It is used to describe qualitatively how several forces lead to a resultant force on that object.

concepts.term: Forces on an isolated object or system
concepts.definition: An isolated object or system is one chosen object, or group of objects treated together, whose forces are considered on their own. Describing the forces acting on it means listing every force that other objects exert on it, such as the weight and the air resistance acting on a falling skydiver.
A single force can be resolved into two components acting at right angles to each other. The two component forces together have the same effect as the single force.

A drawing in which each force is represented by an arrow whose length is set by a stated scale and whose direction is the direction of the force. Vector diagrams are used to illustrate resolution of forces and equilibrium situations, and to determine the resultant of two forces, including both magnitude and direction. Scale drawings only are required.
A situation in which the forces acting on an object are balanced, so that the resultant force is zero. On a scale vector diagram the force arrows, drawn head to tail, form a closed shape.
Forces on an object are balanced when the resultant force on it is zero. Balanced forces are still forces that act on the object — a free body diagram of a balanced object still shows every arrow.

misconceptions.question: Are the weight of an object and the mass of an object the same thing?
misconceptions.correct: Weight is the force acting on an object due to gravity, measured in newtons. Mass is a separate quantity, measured in kilograms, and it is not a force.
misconceptions.misconception: Weight and mass are two words for the same thing — mass is just the downward pull that makes something heavy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language uses 'weight' for what a set of kitchen scales reports, and those scales are marked in kilograms. Students arrive with a single merged idea of heaviness and only later meet two separate physics quantities with two separate units.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the units apart and the quantities stay apart: mass in kilograms, weight in newtons. Mass is the same wherever the object is; weight depends on the gravitational field strength at the point where the object is, and is calculated from W = m g.

misconceptions.question: What unit is weight measured in?
misconceptions.correct: Weight, W, is in newtons, N. Mass, m, is in kilograms, kg.
misconceptions.misconception: Weight is measured in kilograms, because that is what you read off the scales.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Bathroom and kitchen scales are labelled in kilograms and are described as measuring how much you weigh, so the unit kilogram becomes attached to the word weight before physics teaching begins.
misconceptions.correction: Weight is a force, and all forces are measured in newtons. If an answer to a weight calculation comes out in kilograms, the wrong quantity has been found. Weight is measured with a calibrated spring-balance (a newtonmeter), whose scale is in newtons.

misconceptions.question: Does the mass of an object change if it is taken somewhere with a weaker gravitational field?
misconceptions.correct: No. The weight of an object depends on the gravitational field strength at the point where the object is, but the mass does not.
misconceptions.misconception: Things get lighter on the Moon, so their mass must go down as well as their weight.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students who have merged mass and weight into one idea of heaviness have no way to change one without the other. Astronaut footage showing people bounding about reinforces the idea that the object itself has changed.
misconceptions.correction: Only g changes from place to place. In W = m g, m stays the same and g is smaller, so W is smaller. A 6 kg toolbox is still 6 kg on the Moon; only its weight in newtons falls.

misconceptions.question: If two objects end up touching, does the force between them become a contact force?
misconceptions.correct: No. Gravitational, electrostatic and magnetic forces are non-contact forces: they act between objects that are physically separated, and they are still those forces even when the objects happen to be in contact.
misconceptions.misconception: A force only counts as non-contact if the objects are far apart — a magnet stuck to a fridge, or an object resting on the ground, is being held by a contact force.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The classification is taught through a snapshot: are they touching right now? Students apply that test to the situation in front of them rather than to the nature of the force, and gravity in particular is met almost entirely through objects that are resting on something.
misconceptions.correction: Classify by the force, not by the picture. Ask which two objects are interacting: for weight, the Earth and the object, which are separated, so it is non-contact. The normal contact force from the ground is a separate, contact force acting at the same time.

misconceptions.question: Which has a direction — a scalar quantity or a vector quantity?
misconceptions.correct: Scalar quantities have magnitude only. Vector quantities have magnitude and an associated direction.
misconceptions.misconception: A scalar is the one with a direction, and a vector is just a size — or the two words simply mean the same as each other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two terms are new, abstract and introduced together in a single lesson, with nothing in the words themselves to anchor which is which. Students who cannot recall the distinction guess, and a guess is right half the time, which hides the problem.
misconceptions.correction: Anchor it on force, which the specification names as a vector: a 5 N push to the left is not the same as a 5 N push to the right, so force must carry a direction. Mass, time and temperature have magnitude only, so they are scalars.

misconceptions.question: What does the length of a force arrow tell you?
misconceptions.correct: The length of the arrow represents the magnitude of the vector quantity — here, the size of the force in newtons.
misconceptions.misconception: A longer arrow means the force is applied for a longer time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Length is a word students already attach to time in phrases such as 'a long push'. Nothing in the diagram itself forces the size reading, so the everyday meaning of length carries over.
misconceptions.correction: The arrow encodes two things and only two things: length gives the magnitude, and the way it points gives the direction. Duration is not shown on a vector diagram at all.

misconceptions.question: How do you combine two forces that act along the same straight line?
misconceptions.correct: Forces in the same direction are added; forces in opposite directions are subtracted, and the resultant takes the direction of the larger force.
misconceptions.misconception: You add the sizes of the forces together whichever way they point, because a resultant is a total.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word resultant is heard as 'total', and adding is the default operation students reach for when two numbers are given. Direction is treated as decoration on the answer rather than as part of the calculation.
misconceptions.correction: Force is a vector, so direction is part of the arithmetic. Choose one direction as positive, give each force its sign, then add: 15 N left and 9 N right give a resultant of 6 N to the left, not 24 N.

misconceptions.question: If the resultant force on an object is zero, are there any forces acting on it?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Balanced forces are real forces that still act on the object; their resultant is zero because they cancel out.
misconceptions.misconception: A resultant force of zero means there is nothing acting on the object at all, so the free body diagram should be empty.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Zero is read as 'nothing there'. The single number that describes the outcome of the forces is confused with the forces themselves, and diagrams of resting objects are often drawn without arrows in earlier teaching.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish the individual forces from their resultant. A book on a table has its weight acting downwards and the normal contact force from the table acting upwards; both arrows are drawn, equal in length and opposite in direction, and it is only their combination that is zero.

misconceptions.question: Where on a diagram should the weight arrow start?
misconceptions.correct: The weight of an object may be considered to act at a single point referred to as the object's 'centre of mass', so the weight arrow is drawn from that point.
misconceptions.misconception: Weight should be drawn from the bottom of the object, where it presses on the ground.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Weight is experienced as pressure on a surface, so students place the arrow at the point of contact. Diagrams that show a block on a table with arrows crowded at the base reinforce this.
misconceptions.correction: Weight acts on the whole object but may be treated as acting at one point, the centre of mass, so its arrow starts there and points downwards. The force at the base of the object is a different force — the normal contact force from the surface.

misconceptions.question: What sort of quantity is g?
misconceptions.correct: g is the gravitational field strength, measured in newtons per kilogram, N/kg. It is not itself a force.
misconceptions.misconception: g is the force of gravity, so it is measured in newtons and can be added to the mass or to the weight.
misconceptions.whyItArises: g is described in class as 'gravity', a word students already use for the pull they feel. Its unit contains newtons, which makes it look like a force, and it sits alongside two other symbols in W = m g that do stand for a weight and a mass.
misconceptions.correction: Read the unit: newtons per kilogram tells you how many newtons of weight each kilogram of mass gets. It is a rate, not a force. The force in the equation is W, and it is obtained by multiplying, never by adding.

misconceptions.question: When a force is resolved into two components at right angles, how do the components relate to the original force?
misconceptions.correct: The two component forces together have the same effect as the single force. They are not obtained by splitting its magnitude arithmetically.
misconceptions.misconception: The two components must add up in size to the original force, so a 10 N force resolves into 5 N and 5 N.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sharing a number between two parts is the everyday meaning of splitting something up, and students carry that arithmetic across without noticing that the components point in different directions from the original force.
misconceptions.correction: Components are vectors at right angles, so their magnitudes do not simply sum to the original. Judge them from the scale drawing: the two components form the sides of a rectangle whose diagonal is the original force, and each side is shorter than that diagonal.

misconceptions.question: Which forces belong on a free body diagram of an object?
misconceptions.correct: Only the forces that act on that one object.
misconceptions.misconception: You should draw every force in the situation, including the forces that the object pushes back with on other things.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Interactions are taught as producing a force on each of the two objects, so students who have learned that correctly then place both of those forces on one diagram. The diagram is treated as a picture of the whole scene.
misconceptions.correction: Choose the object first, then draw only what the surroundings do to it. A force the object exerts on something else acts on that other object and belongs on that other object's diagram.

misconceptions.question: What does a graph of weight against mass look like for objects at one place?
misconceptions.correct: The weight of an object and the mass of an object are directly proportional, so the graph is a straight line passing through the origin.
misconceptions.misconception: The line curves upwards, or starts above the origin, because weight does not simply keep pace with mass.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet many relationships that are not proportional and treat 'goes up as' and 'is proportional to' as the same claim. Directly proportional is rarely tied back to the two properties that define it — a straight line, and passing through the origin.
misconceptions.correction: Directly proportional means both conditions hold. Check with numbers: if 4 kg weighs 36 N then 12 kg weighs 108 N, exactly three times as much, and 0 kg would weigh 0 N.

misconceptions.question: Is tension a contact force or a non-contact force?
misconceptions.correct: Tension is a contact force. It is one of the examples the specification gives, along with friction, air resistance and the normal contact force.
misconceptions.misconception: Tension must be non-contact, because a rope can pull an object that is a long way from the person doing the pulling.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students judge contact by whether the two ends of the situation are close together, and a long rope makes the load look separated from whatever is pulling it.
misconceptions.correction: Ask which two objects the force acts between. Tension acts between the rope and the object it is attached to, and those two are physically touching, so it is a contact force.

misconceptions.question: What instrument measures weight?
misconceptions.correct: Weight is measured using a calibrated spring-balance (a newtonmeter).
misconceptions.misconception: You measure weight on a balance or a set of scales, like the ones used in a laboratory or a kitchen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A mass balance is the instrument students actually use in lessons, and it is described in everyday speech as weighing things. The word weighing is attached to the wrong instrument long before the two quantities are separated.
misconceptions.correction: A mass balance gives mass in kilograms or grams. To measure weight you need a scale marked in newtons, which is what a calibrated spring-balance — a newtonmeter — provides.

misconceptions.question: How is the resultant of two forces acting at right angles found?
misconceptions.correct: By drawing a scale vector diagram and measuring the resultant from it. The resultant is smaller than the two magnitudes added together.
misconceptions.misconception: You add the two forces, so 3 N and 4 N at right angles give 7 N.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule for forces along a straight line — add them if they act the same way — is generalised to any two forces, because students focus on the numbers rather than on the directions in which the arrows point.
misconceptions.correction: Adding only works along one line. At right angles the two arrows are drawn head to tail and the resultant is the arrow that closes the triangle, measured against the scale: for 3 N and 4 N it comes out as 5 N, not 7 N.

misconceptions.question: Is the gravitational field strength the same everywhere?
misconceptions.correct: No. The weight of an object depends on the gravitational field strength at the point where the object is, and that varies from place to place.
misconceptions.misconception: g is a fixed constant of nature, so an object's weight is a permanent property that never changes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In every calculation students meet on Earth the same value of g is supplied, so it behaves like a constant. Weight is also described as a property of the object in everyday speech, which suggests it travels with it.
misconceptions.correction: Treat g as a property of the place, not of the object. Move the object to a place where g is smaller and its weight falls, even though the object itself is unchanged. This is why the specification states that the value of g will be given in any calculation.

misconceptions.question: Does a force arrow point in the direction the object is moving?
misconceptions.correct: No. The direction of the arrow shows the direction of the force, not the direction of motion.
misconceptions.misconception: Arrows on a diagram show where the object is going, so the arrows and the movement must match.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Arrows are used in many other contexts — maps, flow charts, motion diagrams — to show where something is heading, and that reading is well established before force arrows are introduced.
misconceptions.correction: Read every arrow as a force with a stated direction. A skydiver moving downwards still has an air resistance arrow pointing upwards, because that is the direction in which the air pushes.

misconceptions.question: Why is air resistance a contact force?
misconceptions.correct: Because the object and the air are physically touching as the object moves through it.
misconceptions.misconception: Air resistance is non-contact, because air is not a solid object you can touch.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students take 'physically touching' to mean touching something solid and visible. Air is invisible and is often thought of as empty space rather than as matter that objects push against.
misconceptions.correction: Air is made of particles, and a moving object collides with them constantly. The two interacting objects — the cyclist and the air — are in contact, so air resistance is a contact force, exactly as the specification lists it.

misconceptions.question: Can an object have a force stored inside it?
misconceptions.correct: No. A force is a push or pull that acts on an object due to the interaction with another object, so a force always requires two objects.
misconceptions.misconception: A moving object carries a force inside it that keeps it going and gradually gets used up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language talks about how much force something has when it hits, and about running out of force. This impetus idea is intuitive and predicts everyday motion reasonably well, so it survives teaching.
misconceptions.correction: For every force, name the two objects: which object exerts it and which object it acts on. If only one object can be named, there is no force. Nothing about a force is stored or used up.

misconceptions.question: When two objects interact, does each one experience a force?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The interaction between a pair of objects produces a force on each object.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the active object — the magnet, the person pushing — exerts a force; the other one just receives it and does nothing back.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Interactions are described with an actor and a target: the magnet attracts the nail. The grammar of the sentence assigns all the agency to one object, and students take the physics from the grammar.
misconceptions.correction: Describe the interaction from both ends. The magnet pulls the steel ball, and the steel ball pulls the magnet; both forces are drawn as vectors, one acting on each object.

misconceptions.question: What does centre of mass mean?
misconceptions.correct: It is the single point at which the weight of an object may be considered to act.
misconceptions.misconception: The centre of mass is the heaviest part of the object, where most of the material has collected.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase contains the word mass, so students read it as naming a location where mass is concentrated rather than as a modelling point chosen so that one arrow can stand in for the weight of the whole object.
misconceptions.correction: The centre of mass is a point used to simplify a diagram, not a lump of material. Its purpose is stated in the specification: the weight may be considered to act at that single point.

misconceptions.question: Does resolving a force into components add extra force to the situation?
misconceptions.correct: No. The two component forces together have the same effect as the single force they replace.
misconceptions.misconception: Resolving gives you two forces where there was one, so the object is now being pushed harder than before.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two arrows on a diagram look like more forces than one arrow. Students count arrows rather than tracking that the components are a replacement for the original, not an addition to it.
misconceptions.correction: Components replace the single force; they never act at the same time as it. Draw either the single force or its two components, and the effect on the object is identical.

misconceptions.question: Which way does the resultant of two forces in a straight line act?
misconceptions.correct: In the direction of the larger of the two forces.
misconceptions.misconception: The resultant acts in the direction of whichever force was applied by the person or engine, because that is the force doing the work.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students identify one force as the cause and the other as mere resistance, so the outcome is expected to follow the cause regardless of the sizes involved.
misconceptions.correction: Compare the magnitudes; the physics does not care which force was applied first or by whom. A 15 N force to the left with a 9 N force to the right gives 6 N to the left, whichever of the two was the push.

misconceptions.question: Do you always subtract to find a resultant force?
misconceptions.correct: No. Forces acting in the same direction are added; only forces acting in opposite directions are subtracted.
misconceptions.misconception: Finding a resultant means taking the smaller force away from the larger one, whatever their directions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most introductory examples involve a driving force opposed by friction, so subtraction is practised far more often than addition and becomes the remembered procedure.
misconceptions.correction: Check the directions before choosing the operation. Two forces of 6 N and 4 N both acting to the right give 10 N to the right; the same two forces in opposition give 2 N.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly describes a scalar quantity?

options.text: It has a magnitude but no direction.
options.rationale: Scalar quantities have magnitude only, which is exactly what this option states.

options.text: It has a magnitude and a direction.
options.rationale: This is the definition of a vector quantity, chosen by students who have swapped the two terms.

options.text: It has a direction but no magnitude.
options.rationale: Students who know direction is the distinguishing word but not which term owns it invert the definition completely.

options.text: It has a direction shown by an arrow.
options.rationale: The arrow representation is remembered from the same page of notes and attached to the wrong term.

mcqs.stem: A sledge is pulled across snow. Which of these quantities is a vector?

options.text: a mass of 15 kg loaded onto the sledge
options.rationale: Students who treat mass as the downward pull on the sledge expect it to carry a direction.

options.text: a force of 20 N pulling the sledge north
options.rationale: Force is a vector quantity: this has both a magnitude, 20 N, and an associated direction, north.

options.text: a time of 30 s taken to cross the snow
options.rationale: Any quantity with a number and a unit looks like a vector to a student who has lost the distinction.

options.text: a temperature of −3 °C measured outside
options.rationale: A negative sign is read as a direction, so the minus is mistaken for the 'associated direction' of a vector.

mcqs.stem: Two forces acting on a box are drawn as arrows to the same scale. Arrow P is twice as long as arrow Q. What does this tell you?

options.text: Force P acts for twice as long as force Q.
options.rationale: The everyday link between length and duration is carried over to the diagram.

options.text: Force P moves the box twice as far as Q.
options.rationale: Arrows are read as showing the movement of the object rather than the size of the force.

options.text: Force P is twice the size of force Q.
options.rationale: The length of the arrow represents the magnitude, so double the length means double the force.

options.text: Force P acts at twice the angle of force Q.
options.rationale: Length is confused with the other property the arrow carries, its direction.

mcqs.stem: On a vector diagram, what does the direction in which an arrow points represent?

options.text: the direction in which the object moves
options.rationale: Arrows are widely used elsewhere to show where something is heading, and that reading is imported.

options.text: the length of time the force acts for
options.rationale: Students who attach duration to the arrow attach it to whichever feature they are asked about.

options.text: the order in which the forces were added
options.rationale: Head-to-tail construction suggests to some students that the arrows encode a sequence.

options.text: the direction of the vector quantity
options.rationale: The direction of the arrow represents the direction of the vector quantity.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes what a force is?

options.text: a push or pull on an object caused by another object
options.rationale: A force is a push or pull that acts on an object due to the interaction with another object.

options.text: a push or pull that an object stores up inside it
options.rationale: The impetus idea — that a moving object carries force within it — is intuitive and widely held.

options.text: the amount of matter that an object contains
options.rationale: Students who merge mass and force define one using the other.

options.text: the speed an object gains when it is pushed
options.rationale: The effect of a force is mistaken for the definition of a force.

mcqs.stem: What is the difference between a contact force and a non-contact force?

options.text: Contact forces act only between solids; non-contact forces act through air or through liquids.
options.rationale: Students who think only solids can touch classify air resistance and drag as non-contact.

options.text: Contact forces act when the objects are touching; non-contact forces act when they are separated.
options.rationale: This is the specification's distinction: contact forces — the objects are physically touching; non-contact forces — the objects are physically separated.

options.text: Contact forces are always the larger; non-contact forces are far too weak to be noticed.
options.rationale: Forces that need touching feel real and strong, so forces across a gap are assumed to be feeble.

options.text: Contact forces act instantly; non-contact forces take time to reach the other object.
options.rationale: A gap is imagined as something the force has to travel across, so a delay is invented.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is an example of a contact force?

options.text: the magnetic force on a steel nail
options.rationale: A nail stuck to a magnet is touching it, so the force is reclassified from the picture rather than from its nature.

options.text: the weight of a stone resting on soil
options.rationale: Weight is met almost entirely through objects resting on surfaces, so it is read as a force of contact with the ground.

options.text: the tension in a rope towing a boat
options.rationale: Tension is one of the contact forces named by the specification; the rope and the boat are physically touching.

options.text: the electrostatic force on a charge
options.rationale: Electrostatic effects are demonstrated by rubbing objects together, so contact becomes part of the mental image.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is an example of a non-contact force?

options.text: the tension in a steel cable holding up a lift car
options.rationale: A long cable makes the load look separated from whatever is pulling it.

options.text: the air resistance on a cyclist riding down a hill
options.rationale: Air is treated as empty space rather than as matter the cyclist is in contact with.

options.text: the friction between a car tyre and the road below
options.rationale: Chosen by students selecting whichever force they associate least with a deliberate push or pull.

options.text: the electrostatic force between two charged spheres
options.rationale: Electrostatic force is named by the specification as a non-contact force; the two spheres are physically separated.

mcqs.stem: Air resistance acts on a cyclist. Why is air resistance classed as a contact force?

options.text: The air is physically touching the moving cyclist.
options.rationale: The two interacting objects, the cyclist and the air, are physically touching, which is the specification's test for a contact force.

options.text: The air acts on the cyclist from a distance away.
options.rationale: Students who do not count air as matter describe it as acting across a gap, which would make it non-contact.

options.text: The force is caused by gravity pulling the air down.
options.rationale: Any force that resists motion is attributed to gravity, the one non-contact force students know well.

options.text: The force exists only while the cyclist is moving.
options.rationale: A true statement about air resistance offered as the reason for its classification, which it is not.

mcqs.stem: Two forces of 5 N act on a box. Why is stating '5 N' not enough to describe each force fully?

options.text: Force is a scalar, so only the size of the force matters.
options.rationale: Students who have swapped the two definitions classify force as a scalar.

options.text: Force is a vector, so each force also has a direction.
options.rationale: Force is a vector quantity, so a full description needs magnitude and an associated direction.

options.text: Force is a vector, so it must be measured in kilograms.
options.rationale: The unit of force is confused with the unit of mass, so the newton value is judged wrong.

options.text: Force is a scalar, so the two forces have to cancel out.
options.rationale: Equal magnitudes are assumed to imply cancellation without checking direction.

mcqs.stem: A magnet is held near a steel ball. Which statement describes the interaction correctly?

options.text: Only the magnet exerts a force, because it is magnetic.
options.rationale: The magnet is cast as the actor and the ball as the passive target of the sentence.

options.text: Neither object feels a force until the two of them touch.
options.rationale: Students who require contact for a force to exist deny any force across the gap.

options.text: The magnet pulls the ball and the ball pulls the magnet.
options.rationale: The interaction between the pair of objects produces a force on each object, and both are drawn as vectors.

options.text: The ball pushes the magnet away as the magnet pulls it.
options.rationale: Both forces are identified, but one direction is reversed so that the pair opposes rather than attracts.

mcqs.stem: What is the weight of an object?

options.text: the amount of matter contained in the object
options.rationale: Weight is defined as mass by students who have merged the two quantities.

options.text: the force the object needs to start it moving
options.rationale: Weight is treated as the store of force an object has for moving.

options.text: the number of kilograms the object measures
options.rationale: The reading from a set of scales, in kilograms, is taken to be the weight.

options.text: the force acting on the object due to gravity
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition of weight.

mcqs.stem: Why does an object have weight when it is close to the Earth?

options.text: because it is in the gravitational field around the Earth
options.rationale: The force of gravity close to the Earth is due to the gravitational field around the Earth.

options.text: because it is in contact with the surface of the Earth
options.rationale: Gravity is reclassified as a contact force acting through the ground.

options.text: because the mass inside it pulls it down to the ground
options.rationale: Mass is treated as a downward force in its own right rather than as a separate quantity.

options.text: because the air above it presses down on top of it
options.rationale: A real downward push is substituted for the gravitational field as the cause of weight.

mcqs.stem: An astronaut takes a 6 kg toolbox from the Earth to the Moon, where the gravitational field strength is smaller. What happens to the toolbox?

options.text: Its mass becomes smaller and its weight stays the same.
options.rationale: Students who know something must change but have the quantities swapped alter the mass instead.

options.text: Its mass stays at 6 kg and its weight becomes smaller.
options.rationale: Weight depends on the gravitational field strength at the point where the object is; mass does not.

options.text: Both its mass and its weight are made smaller as well.
options.rationale: With mass and weight merged into one idea of heaviness, both must fall together.

options.text: Both its mass and its weight stay at exactly the same.
options.rationale: g is treated as a universal constant, so weight is taken to be a fixed property of the object.

mcqs.stem: A crate has a mass of 60 kg. The gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. What is the weight of the crate?

options.rationale: The mass is quoted as the weight, with only the unit changed.
g is treated as a force to be added on rather than as a multiplier.
The mass is divided by g instead of multiplied, a common reversal when the equation is not written out first.

mcqs.stem: A bag has a weight of 245 N. The gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. What is the mass of the bag?

options.text: 245 kg
options.rationale: The newton value is relabelled in kilograms because weight and mass are treated as one quantity.
The equation is used unrearranged, multiplying by g when the mass is the unknown.

options.text: 235 kg
options.rationale: g is subtracted as though it were a force in newtons.

options.text: 25 kg
options.rationale: Rearranging W = m g gives m = W / g = 245 / 9.8 = 25 kg.

mcqs.stem: In the equation W = m g, which units are used for W and for m?

options.text: W in newtons and m in kilograms
options.rationale: The specification gives weight, W, in newtons, N and mass, m, in kilograms, kg.

options.text: W in kilograms and m in newtons
options.rationale: The unit read off everyday scales is attached to weight, forcing mass into the other unit.

options.text: W in newtons and m in grams
options.rationale: Grams are the familiar laboratory unit, and the conversion to kilograms is overlooked.

options.text: W and m both in kilograms
options.rationale: If weight and mass are the same quantity they must share a unit.

mcqs.stem: What is the unit of gravitational field strength?

options.text: newtons, the same unit as any force
options.rationale: g is thought of as the force of gravity, so it takes the unit of a force.

options.text: newtons per kilogram, written N/kg
options.rationale: The specification gives gravitational field strength, g, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg.

options.text: kilograms, the same unit as the mass
options.rationale: Every gravity-related quantity is assigned the unit students associate with heaviness.

options.text: kilograms per newton, written kg/N
options.rationale: The right two units are recalled but the ratio is inverted.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the centre of mass of an object?

options.text: the point inside the object at which it is heaviest of all
options.rationale: The word mass in the name is read as marking where material is concentrated.

options.text: the point where the object touches the ground beneath it
options.rationale: Weight is felt as pressure on a surface, so its point of action is placed at the base.

options.text: the single point at which the weight may be taken to act
options.rationale: The weight of an object may be considered to act at a single point referred to as the object's centre of mass.

options.text: the point exactly halfway up the height of the object
options.rationale: The centre of mass is reduced to a purely geometric midpoint of the shape.

mcqs.stem: The weight of an object and the mass of an object are directly proportional. What shape is a graph of weight against mass for objects measured at one place?

options.text: a curve that becomes steeper as the mass rises
options.rationale: Students who read 'increases with' as any rising relationship expect a curve.

options.text: a straight line that starts above the origin
options.rationale: The straight-line half of the definition is remembered but the origin condition is dropped.

options.text: a horizontal line at one fixed value of weight
options.rationale: Weight is treated as a constant property that does not depend on mass at all.

options.text: a straight line passing through the origin
options.rationale: Directly proportional quantities give a straight line through the origin.

mcqs.stem: On a planet, a rock of mass 4 kg has a weight of 36 N. What is the weight of a 12 kg rock on the same planet?

options.rationale: Weight and mass are directly proportional: the mass is three times larger, so the weight is 3 × 36 = 108 N.
The extra 8 kg is added straight on to the 36 N, treating kilograms and newtons as the same quantity.
The ratio is applied the wrong way round by a student not holding on to what proportional means.
The weight is multiplied by the new mass, 4 × 36, instead of by the ratio of the masses.

mcqs.stem: Which instrument is used to measure the weight of an object?

options.text: a top-pan laboratory balance reading in grams
options.rationale: This is the instrument students actually use in lessons and describe as weighing things.

options.text: a calibrated spring-balance, called a newtonmeter
options.rationale: The specification states that weight is measured using a calibrated spring-balance (a newtonmeter).

options.text: a set of bathroom scales marked in kilograms
options.rationale: Everyday weighing is done on scales marked in kilograms, which fixes the wrong unit and instrument.

options.text: a measuring cylinder part filled with water
options.rationale: Displacement is recalled as a way of finding something about an object, but it gives volume, not weight.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the resultant force on an object?

options.text: the total of the sizes of all the forces acting on the object
options.rationale: Resultant is heard as 'total', so the magnitudes are summed regardless of direction.

options.text: the force that is left once the object has stopped moving
options.rationale: Resultant is confused with what remains, and a stationary object is assumed to have none.

options.text: the single force with the same effect as all the forces together
options.rationale: A number of forces may be replaced by a single force that has the same effect as all the original forces acting together.

options.text: the largest of the forces that are acting on the object
options.rationale: The force that appears to dominate is taken to be the resultant on its own.

mcqs.stem: A trolley is pushed with a force of 6 N to the right. A second force of 4 N also acts to the right. What is the resultant force on the trolley?

options.text: 2 N to the right
options.rationale: Subtraction is applied automatically because most practised examples involve opposing forces.

options.text: 24 N to the right
options.rationale: The two values are multiplied, a slip made when the operation is chosen by habit rather than by direction.

options.text: 10 N to the left
options.rationale: The magnitudes are combined correctly but the direction is not tracked through the working.

options.text: 10 N to the right
options.rationale: Forces acting in the same direction along a straight line are added: 6 + 4 = 10 N to the right.

mcqs.stem: A box has a force of 15 N acting on it to the left and a force of 9 N acting to the right. What is the resultant force on the box?

options.text: 6 N to the left
options.rationale: Forces in opposite directions are subtracted: 15 − 9 = 6 N, acting in the direction of the larger force.

options.text: 24 N to the left
options.rationale: The sizes are added because resultant is read as total.

options.text: 6 N to the right
options.rationale: The magnitude is right but the direction is taken from the force treated as the applied push.

options.text: 24 N to the right
options.rationale: Both errors combine: magnitudes added and the direction taken from the smaller force.

mcqs.stem: A skydiver is falling through the air. Which pair of forces acts on the skydiver?

options.text: weight downwards and the diver's push on the air
options.rationale: A force the skydiver exerts on something else is placed on the skydiver's own diagram.

options.text: weight downwards and air resistance upwards
options.rationale: These are the two forces other objects exert on the isolated skydiver: gravity acting downwards and the air pushing upwards.

options.text: air resistance upwards and a force of falling
options.rationale: Motion itself is treated as a force the moving object carries.

options.text: weight downwards and air resistance downwards
options.rationale: The air resistance arrow is turned to follow the direction of motion rather than the push of the air.

mcqs.stem: A free body diagram of a book resting on a table shows two arrows of equal length pointing in opposite directions. What does this show?

options.text: There are no forces acting on the book at all now.
options.rationale: A zero resultant is read as an absence of forces rather than as their cancellation.

options.text: The two forces cancel, so the book has no weight.
options.rationale: Cancelling the arrows is taken to remove the weight itself, a property of the book.

options.text: The forces are balanced, so the resultant force is zero.
options.rationale: Equal and opposite forces are balanced, and the free body diagram shows the resultant force to be zero.

options.text: The resultant force acts upwards on the resting book.
options.rationale: The upward arrow is judged to win because the book is held up by the table.

mcqs.stem: Which forces should be drawn on a free body diagram of a car?

options.text: the forces on the car and those it exerts
options.rationale: Both halves of an interaction pair are drawn on the same object's diagram.

options.text: only the forces that make the car speed up
options.rationale: Forces are equated with the causes of motion, so resisting forces are left out.

options.text: every force acting anywhere near the car
options.rationale: The diagram is treated as a picture of the whole scene rather than of one object.

options.text: only the forces that act on the car itself
options.rationale: A free body diagram shows the forces acting on the one chosen object and nothing else.

mcqs.stem: A single force is resolved into two components acting at right angles to each other. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The two components together have the same effect as the single force.
options.rationale: This is the specification's statement: the two component forces together have the same effect as the single force.

options.text: The two component sizes must add up to the size of the force.
options.rationale: Splitting is taken to be arithmetic sharing of the magnitude between two parts.

options.text: Adding the two components gives a force larger than before.
options.rationale: Two arrows look like more force than one, so the object is thought to be pushed harder.

options.text: The two components always act in the same direction as each other.
options.rationale: The defining condition — that the components are at right angles — is not held on to.

mcqs.stem: A scale drawing is used to find the resultant of a 3 N force and a 4 N force acting at right angles to each other. What is the magnitude of the resultant?

options.text: 7 N
options.rationale: The straight-line rule for adding forces is applied to forces at right angles.

options.text: 5 N
options.rationale: Drawn head to tail to scale, the arrow closing the triangle measures 5 N.

options.text: 1 N
options.rationale: Subtraction is used by default whenever two forces are not obviously in the same direction.
The two magnitudes are multiplied, an operation reached for when no drawing is attempted.

mcqs.stem: A scale vector diagram is drawn for the forces acting on an object that is in equilibrium. What does the completed diagram look like?

options.text: The diagram is left empty, as no forces act on the object at all.
options.rationale: A zero resultant is taken to mean there is nothing to draw.

options.text: The arrows all point one way, so their sizes are added together.
options.rationale: Combining forces is remembered as summing magnitudes, whatever the directions.

options.text: The arrows form a closed shape, showing the resultant force is zero.
options.rationale: In equilibrium the forces are balanced, so the head-to-tail arrows close and no resultant arrow remains.

options.text: The longest arrow shows the direction the object is moving in.
options.rationale: Arrows are read as showing motion rather than the forces acting.
